topStories.headline: Demolition Permits Filed for Potrero Yard, Marking First Physical Step in $612M Mission District Overhaul
topStories.dek: New permits filed September 10 set the stage for demolition of the century-old Muni bus yard, though the wrecking ball won't swing until early 2027.
topStories.body:
Demolition permits were filed September 10 for the 4.4-acre site at 2500 Mariposa Street, the first tangible paperwork milestone in the long-running effort to replace San Francisco's oldest bus storage facility. The filing moves the Potrero Yard Modernization Project — a $612 million overhaul unanimously approved by the Board of Supervisors on March 24 — closer to its next phase of site preparation.

The project will gut and replace a bus maintenance and storage complex that has served Muni for more than 111 years. According to the SFMTA's project page, the agency spent the remainder of 2026 finalizing its move-out from the yard, conducting site due diligence, and removing overhead lines. Prime contractor Webcor is expected to begin full demolition in early 2027, with the new facility scheduled to open in 2030.

The redevelopment has been contentious in the Mission. The SFMTA board voted in March to dramatically scale back the project's affordable housing component — from an originally proposed 465 units to just 100. Community members and housing advocates objected to the reduction, with Calle 24 Latino Cultural District president Erick Arguello saying at the March board meeting, "We feel a little used." The 100 remaining units will be studios to three-bedroom apartments reserved for households earning up to 80 percent of the area median income.

For Mission District residents, the demolition permit filing represents both a long-awaited physical milestone and a continuing source of frustration over what was lost. SF YIMBY, which first covered the project in 2020 when it was conceptual, noted that the new permits mark a significant turning point. The 16th Street BART station is about a 17-minute walk from the site.

topStories.headline: Judge Throws Out All Charges Against 'Stud Alley 18' Arrested at Pride Street Party
topStories.dek: A visiting Superior Court judge dismissed charges against all 18 defendants on September 14, finding police had not properly issued a dispersal order before making arrests.
topStories.body:
A judge dismissed all charges on September 14 against 18 people who were arrested at the "Stud Alley" party on June 27 — the Saturday night of San Francisco Pride weekend — after determining that police had not issued a proper dispersal order immediately before the arrests. The ruling closed a nearly three-month ordeal that defendants said had targeted the city's queer community.

District Attorney Brooke Jenkins had charged all 18 with unlawful assembly, failure to comply with a dispersal order, and resisting arrest. But visiting Santa Barbara Superior Court Judge Brian Hill, presiding over a packed Hall of Justice courtroom, found the evidence insufficient. Body-camera footage and internal SFPD documents, obtained earlier in September by defense attorneys and reported first by Mission Local, showed that officers had issued a dispersal order more than an hour before the arrests — and before the party had moved to a new location — rather than immediately prior. The judge found that for all but one defendant there was, at most, "minimal resistance."

"At this point, I think that there is ample reason to conclude that a motion to dismiss should be granted in the interest of justice," Hill said in court. He reviewed each defendant individually and found that all but one had no prior criminal record. Several had lost employment because of the arrest, and one defendant faced potential visa complications.

More than 100 people had been dancing in the alley near the former home of the Stud bar in SoMa when police moved in. Mission Local's reporting on the police documents was credited by defense attorneys as pivotal to the outcome.

topStories.headline: San Francisco Loses Another Newsroom: The Frisc Shutting Down by End of September
topStories.dek: The nonprofit outlet, which focused on housing and civic issues for nearly a decade, announced it has run out of money — the latest blow to local journalism in a city already watching El Tecolote struggle.
topStories.body:
The Frisc, a nonprofit San Francisco news site founded in 2017 with a focus on housing, transit, and civic accountability, announced this month that it will cease operations by the end of September. Editor-in-chief and co-founder Alex Lash cited financial difficulties and said the site had "pretty much run out of money," telling the SF Standard he was paying for the publication's farewell party out of his own pocket.

The closure follows the announcement last week in these pages that El Tecolote — California's longest-running bilingual newspaper — lost most of its staff. Together, the two closures underscore a deepening crisis in Mission-area and citywide local journalism. Lash launched The Frisc in 2016 alongside fellow journalists Anthony Lazarus, Barry Owen, and designer Jeremy LaCroix, after identifying what he saw as a gap in San Francisco's media landscape.

Over nearly a decade, The Frisc grew to cover housing, education, transit, city government, and the environment. It won two awards from the Society of Professional Journalists NorCal chapter in 2025. Freelancer Ida Mojadad, one of the award recipients, said the loss meant "a less informed city." Funding became increasingly difficult to secure in 2025, Lash told The Standard, partly because competition for a limited pool of nonprofit journalism dollars intensified after federal support for public radio stations like KQED ended.

Lash wrote in his farewell note: "Nonprofit media in the best of times is no easy lift. These are not the best of times." The site's archives are expected to remain online as a public record.

events.title: 75th Annual San Francisco Greek Food Festival

events.description: Three days of homemade Greek food, traditional folk dancing, live music, and community celebration marking the festival's 75th year. Free admission.

moreNews.headline: Foundation Work Underway at 2918 Mission Street, Where 75 Apartments Are Finally Rising
moreNews.body: Construction is underway at the site of the former Wash Club laundromat at 2918 Mission Street, a property that became one of the most symbolically charged addresses in San Francisco's decade-long housing wars. Developer Cresleigh Homes, which acquired the site in April 2019 for $13.5 million, began site preparation and foundation work in August 2026, according to the SF Chronicle. The eight-story building will yield 75 rental apartments and approximately 7,000 square feet of ground-floor retail. Vertical construction is expected to begin in 2027. The original property owner spent years in legal battles over the city's approval process before selling to Cresleigh.

restaurants.name: El Farolito

restaurants.name: Foreign Cinema

restaurants.name: Loló
restaurants.description: A neighborhood favorite serving creative Mexican small plates, mezcal cocktails, and seasonal dishes in a lively, colorful setting on 22nd Street.

restaurants.name: Lolinda

restaurants.name: Farmhouse Kitchen Thai Cuisine
restaurants.description: A highly rated Thai restaurant on Florida Street serving refined, authentic Thai dishes in an elegantly decorated dining room inspired by traditional Thai farm houses.

restaurants.name: Penny Roma

restaurants.name: Trick Dog
restaurants.description: An award-winning craft cocktail bar on 20th Street with a rotating, thematic menu of inventive drinks and a convivial neighborhood atmosphere.

restaurants.name: El Rio
restaurants.description: A legendary Mission bar since 1977 known for its large outdoor patio, live music, and inclusive, community-spirited atmosphere on Mission Street.

restaurants.name: Al Carajo
restaurants.description: A neighborhood gem on 22nd Street celebrated by many as the home of the best breakfast burrito in San Francisco, made with fresh, quality ingredients.

restaurants.name: Bon, Nene
restaurants.description: A compact, warmly reviewed Japanese bistro in the Mission serving gyudon, Japanese curry, and comfort-focused dishes at fair prices.

restaurants.name: Sangria & Salt
restaurants.description: A vibrant Mission District spot known for housemade sangria, fresh ceviche, jerk chicken tacos, and warm, owner-led hospitality.

restaurants.name: Emmy's Spaghetti Shack
restaurants.description: A beloved neighborhood fixture on Mission Street serving generous portions of spaghetti, meatballs, and Italian-American comfort classics in a casual, no-frills setting.

restaurants.name: The Front Porch
restaurants.description: A cozy neighborhood spot serving Southern-inspired comfort food including fried chicken, mac and cheese, and craft cocktails in a relaxed Bernal Heights setting.

restaurants.name: Royal Cuckoo Organ Bar
restaurants.description: A Mission Street institution featuring nightly live vintage organ music, craft cocktails, and a warm, eccentric atmosphere that draws devoted regulars from across the city.

restaurants.name: Flour & Water Pasta Shop
restaurants.description: The walk-in, counter-service sibling of Flour + Water on 18th Street, offering fresh handmade pasta dishes and pastries for a quick, high-quality meal.

restaurants.name: Ritual Coffee Roasters (Valencia)
restaurants.description: One of the original Bay Area third-wave coffee roasters, Ritual's Valencia Street location is a neighborhood hub for carefully sourced and roasted single-origin coffees.

restaurants.name: El Farolito (Outer Mission)
restaurants.description: The Outer Mission location of the beloved El Farolito taqueria chain, serving legendary super burritos and tacos at the southern end of Mission Street.

restaurants.name: Dandelion Chocolate Café
restaurants.description: A craft chocolate maker on Valencia Street sourcing cacao directly from farms and making each bar in small batches on-site, with a factory store and tasting café open to visitors.

hotels.name: Inn San Francisco
hotels.description: A beautifully restored 1872 Italianate Victorian mansion on South Van Ness Avenue operating as a distinguished B&B, with a garden, hot tub, and individually decorated rooms.

shops.name: Paxton Gate
shops.description: A Mission District landmark since 1992, Paxton Gate stocks taxidermy, fossils, carnivorous plants, skulls, crystals, and natural science ephemera at 824 Valencia St.

shops.name: 826 Valencia (Pirate Supply Store)
shops.type: Youth writing nonprofit and pirate supply store
shops.description: The whimsical Pirate Supply Store front funds 826 Valencia's free youth writing and tutoring programs, making it one of the most community-rooted and quirky shops in the city.

shops.name: Dog Eared Books
shops.description: A beloved Valencia Street independent bookstore offering a thoughtfully curated selection of new, used, and hard-to-find titles with a strong local and community focus.

shops.name: City Art Gallery & Co-op
shops.description: A worker-owned cooperative gallery on Valencia Street showcasing and selling affordable original artwork by a rotating roster of Bay Area artists.

shops.name: Bi-Rite Market
shops.type: Neighborhood grocery and specialty food market
shops.description: A Mission District institution on 18th Street offering high-quality local and artisan groceries, prepared foods, and a celebrated cheese counter for over two decades.

shops.name: Bi-Rite Creamery
shops.description: The wildly popular sister creamery to Bi-Rite Market, churning small-batch organic ice creams in flavors like salted caramel and ricanelas, with lines perpetually stretching down 18th Street.

shops.name: Dandelion Chocolate
shops.description: A craft chocolate maker on Valencia Street that sources cacao directly from farms and makes each bar in small batches on-site, with a factory store open to visitors.

shops.name: Precita Eyes Mural Arts Visitor Center
shops.type: Mural arts center and gift shop
shops.description: The Mission's foremost community mural organization sells prints, cards, and art supplies from its 24th Street visitor center, and leads guided walking tours of the neighborhood's legendary murals.

shops.name: Alamo Drafthouse New Mission
shops.description: The restored 1916 New Mission Theatre, now a dine-in cinema screening first-run and repertory films with a full food and cocktail menu served in-seat.

artEntertainment.name: Dance Mission Theater
artEntertainment.description: A women-led, multicultural nonprofit performance venue and dance school on 24th Street, home to Dance Brigade and hosting roughly 1,500 students weekly across 50-plus classes.

artEntertainment.name: SF Community Music Center (CMC)
artEntertainment.type: Community music school and concert hall
artEntertainment.description: A Mission District nonprofit music school founded in 1921, offering affordable instruction and hosting concerts and community events in a beautifully restored Victorian carriage house concert hall.

artEntertainment.name: Alamo Drafthouse New Mission
artEntertainment.description: The lovingly restored 1916 New Mission Theatre, now a dine-in cinema screening first-run and repertory films with a full menu and cocktails served in-seat.

artEntertainment.name: The Portal Cinema (Opening Fall 2026)
artEntertainment.description: A forthcoming 49-seat nonprofit arthouse cinema at 3293 Mission St. in Bernal Heights, targeting a late-October or November 2026 opening with indie, global, and repertory programming in digital, 35mm, and 16mm formats.

artEntertainment.name: Bernal Heights Outdoor Cinema
artEntertainment.description: A volunteer-driven annual festival since 2004 presenting free screenings of local filmmakers' short films in Bernal Heights parks and community spaces each September.

artEntertainment.name: Foreign Cinema (Courtyard Screenings)
artEntertainment.description: Foreign Cinema has projected foreign and independent films nightly against the wall of its heated outdoor courtyard since 1999, pairing California-Mediterranean cuisine with cinema.

artEntertainment.name: 500 Capp Street Foundation
artEntertainment.description: The preserved home and studio of pioneering conceptual artist David Ireland, open to the public as a museum celebrating his legacy and the Mission's art history.

artEntertainment.name: Galería de la Raza
artEntertainment.description: Founded in 1970, Galería de la Raza is a pioneering nonprofit gallery on 24th Street dedicated to exhibiting and promoting Chicanx and Latinx art and culture in the heart of the Mission.

artEntertainment.name: Mission Cultural Center for Latino Arts
artEntertainment.description: A city-funded cultural center on Mission Street presenting visual art exhibitions, performing arts, and arts education programs for the Latino community since 1977.

artEntertainment.name: Precita Eyes Muralists
artEntertainment.description: The Mission's foremost community mural organization offers guided walking tours of the neighborhood's legendary murals, a gallery of mural art, and ongoing arts education programs from its 24th Street visitor center.

gymsRecreation.name: Mission Yoga
gymsRecreation.description: Serving the Mission District since 2001, Mission Yoga offers hot yoga, Hot Pilates, Buti Yoga, Yin Yoga, sound baths, and breathwork at its 2415 Mission St. location.

gymsRecreation.name: HAUM SF – Mission Studio
gymsRecreation.description: A spacious and light-filled Mission District yoga collective offering Hatha, Vinyasa, Restorative, and Slow Flow classes in a welcoming, inclusive atmosphere.

gymsRecreation.name: AstaYoga
gymsRecreation.description: A Mission District yoga studio offering instruction in Rocket and Ashtanga Vinyasa yoga, praised for knowledgeable instructors and a community-centered atmosphere.

gymsRecreation.name: 24th Street Yoga
gymsRecreation.description: A neighborhood yoga studio on 24th Street in the heart of the Mission offering a full schedule of classes for all skill levels in a community-oriented setting.

gymsRecreation.name: MX3 Fitness (Mission)
gymsRecreation.description: An LGBTQ+-owned and operated fitness studio in the Mission offering personal training and group fitness classes, proudly serving San Francisco since 2016.

gymsRecreation.name: Mission Dolores Park
gymsRecreation.description: San Francisco's beloved Dolores Park offers tennis courts, a playground, two soccer fields, a basketball court, and iconic hilltop views — the neighborhood's de facto outdoor living room.

gymsRecreation.name: Bernal Heights Park
gymsRecreation.type: Hilltop open space with off-leash dog area
gymsRecreation.description: The iconic open-space hilltop park atop Bernal Heights offers panoramic 360-degree views of San Francisco, a beloved off-leash dog area, and trails winding around the rocky summit.

gymsRecreation.name: Bernal Heights Playground
gymsRecreation.description: Newly renovated and reopened in 2026 by SF Recreation and Parks, this fully accessible and modernized playground features new ADA-compliant equipment built with community input.

gymsRecreation.name: Precita Park
gymsRecreation.description: A beloved community green space at the foot of Bernal Heights with lawns, a playground, and a community garden, frequently used as a venue for outdoor cinema and neighborhood gatherings.

gymsRecreation.name: Cayuga Park
gymsRecreation.description: A singular park beneath the BART tracks in the Outer Mission featuring dense vegetation, over 100 whimsical wood sculptures carved by the park's creator, a small baseball field, and tennis courts.
